title: London's safeguarded wharves demand and capacity research
gist: GLA-commissioned Oxford Economics research forecasts a potential shortfall in London's safeguarded wharf capacity by 2050, with construction-materials demand alone exceeding capacity by 622,000 tonnes. It stresses that location, commodity capability and efficiency of wharf capacity matter as much as its total, amid pressure to release riverside land for housing.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics forecasts London's safeguarded wharves face a potential capacity shortfall by 2050, with demand for construction materials alone exceeding available capacity by 622,000 tonnes.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Constrained aggregates/materials logistics into London could raise construction input costs and favour existing wharf operators.
insights.quote: demand for construction materials alone forecast to exceed available capacity by 622,000 tonnes

insights.claim: Pressure to release London riverside land for housing and other development is in tension with the need to keep safeguarded wharves that supply materials and take freight off congested roads.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Wharf safeguarding decisions affect riverside property development supply and wharf asset scarcity value.

insights.claim: Closing London wharves would push freight onto congested roads and raise transport emissions, since wharves currently move goods by river.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Wharf closures carry hidden congestion/emissions costs relevant to planning and logistics operators.

themes.theme: Location matters as much as volume

insights.claim: Oxford Economics finds regional differences across the North East, South East and West regions of the Thames mean the location of future London wharf capacity could matter as much as its overall level.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Aggregate capacity figures can mislead; scarcity is regional, so well-located wharves are more valuable.
insights.quote: the location of future capacity could be just as important as its overall level

insights.claim: The GLA research uses ten years of Port of London Authority freight data, industrial demand forecasts and wharf operator interviews across seven commodity groups, including construction materials, agricultural bulks, metals, petroleum products and waste.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Indicates the evidence base that will shape London's wharf safeguarding policy.

insights.claim: Future London wharf demand and capacity are uncertain due to major infrastructure projects, wharf closures and changing river connectivity, per the GLA-commissioned research.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Large London infrastructure projects can swing wharf demand; monitor project pipeline and closure decisions.

insights.claim: The research argues London's wharf policy should consider not only total capacity but where it is located, which commodities it can handle and how efficiently it is used.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Efficiency upgrades at existing wharves may substitute for new capacity, favouring operators that invest.
